result: Non-lesional skin from human lupus (DLE) and three murine lupus models (MRL/lpr, B6.Sle1yaa, IMQ) share an IFN-rich environment characterized by upregulation of IFN-I pathways, IFN-stimulated genes, and IRF transcription factors, though the magnitude and specific features vary across models.
evaluation: Claims C4, C27-C73 collectively demonstrate through transcriptomic analysis (microarray and RNAseq) that non-lesional skin across human DLE and three murine models exhibits IFN signatures. The data include QuSAGE pathway analysis, GSVA, and differential gene expression showing consistent upregulation of IFN-I pathways and ISGs. The findings are supported by multiple figures (1-4) showing PCA, volcano plots, heatmaps, and pathway enrichment analyses with appropriate statistical thresholds (FDR<0.05).

result: Lesional DLE skin shows enrichment of immune cell gene sets (plasma cells, T cells, myeloid cells, neutrophils, pDCs), inflammatory cytokine signatures (IL12, IL21, IL23, TNF, IFN), and dramatic LC gene set de-enrichment compared to controls and psoriatic skin.
evaluation: Claims C35-C40 are supported by GSVA analysis shown in Figure 1E-F with appropriate statistical testing. The findings are consistent with cited previous studies and the original study characterizing these samples. The LC de-enrichment is more dramatic than in psoriatic skin, providing a disease-specific comparison.

result: MRL/lpr mice show enrichment of inflammatory cell and cytokine gene sets including T cells, myeloid cells, neutrophils, pDCs, IFN, IL1, IL21, and TNF, with enriched keratinocyte signature but unchanged LC signature.
evaluation: Claims C59-C61 are supported by GSVA analysis in Figure 3A using lupus-relevant murine gene sets. The unchanged LC signature is consistent with previous findings (Shipman et al., 2018) showing unchanged LC numbers in MRL/lpr mice, providing internal consistency.

result: IFN-I (IFN-κ and IFN-β) inhibits LC ADAM17 sheddase activity in both murine and human LCs ex vivo and in vivo, with minimal effects on ADAM17 protein expression or LC numbers, and this inhibition is JAK1/3-dependent.
evaluation: Claims C5, C74-C83 are supported by experimental data in Figure 5 showing dose-dependent reduction in UVR-induced TNFR1 loss (sheddase activity readout) with IFN-κ (~40% reduction ex vivo, 57% in vivo) and IFN-β (62% in human LCs). The assay was validated using LCAd17 mice (C74-C75). Effects on ADAM17 protein were modest (8-9%) and LC numbers unchanged. Tofacitinib abrogated the effect, confirming JAK-dependence. Sample sizes (n=3-10) and statistical tests (paired/unpaired t-tests) are appropriate.

result: IFNAR blockade restores LC ADAM17 sheddase activity in three lupus models (MRL/lpr, B6.Sle1yaa, IMQ) without consistent effects on ADAM17 protein expression or LC numbers, demonstrating that IFN-I specifically regulates sheddase function.
evaluation: Claims C6, C84-C95 are supported by experimental data in Figure 6 and Table 1 showing that anti-IFNAR treatment restored LC ADAM17 sheddase activity across all three models (42-63% reduction in disease, restored by anti-IFNAR) without consistently affecting protein levels or LC numbers. The consistency across models and the uncoupling of activity from expression/cell numbers (Table 1) strongly support the conclusion. Sample sizes (n=3-9) and statistical methods are appropriate.

result: Anti-IFNAR-mediated restoration of LC ADAM17 sheddase function reduces photosensitive responses (ear swelling, epidermal permeability, inflammatory infiltrates) in lupus mice, and this effect is dependent on EGFR signaling and LC ADAM17.
evaluation: Claims C7, C96-C108 are supported by experimental data in Figure 7 showing that anti-IFNAR at 125 μg/dose reduced UVR-induced ear swelling, epidermal permeability, and neutrophil/monocyte infiltration in MRL/lpr and IMQ mice. The EGFR inhibitor PD168393 abrogated these effects (C104), and anti-IFNAR failed to reduce monocyte accumulation in LCAd17 mice lacking LC ADAM17 (C108), demonstrating dependence on EGFR signaling and LC ADAM17. The dose-response findings (C96-C101) showing that high-dose anti-IFNAR increased photosensitivity in control mice are consistent with cited literature on IFNAR deficiency effects.

result: UVR-induced LC ROS production is reduced in lupus model mice, restored by anti-IFNAR treatment, and is predominantly cytoplasmic in origin.
evaluation: Claims C8-C10, C109-C111 are supported by experimental data in Figure 8 showing reduced UVR-induced ROS in IMQ mice, restoration by anti-IFNAR, and cytoplasmic (CellROX) rather than mitochondrial (MitoSOX) origin. Sample sizes (n=5-6) and statistical tests are appropriate. This provides a mechanistic link between IFN-I and ADAM17 activity, as ROS is a known mediator of ADAM17 function.

result: IFN-I promotes photosensitivity at least in part by inhibiting UVR-induced LC ADAM17 sheddase function, likely through reduction of LC ROS generation.
evaluation: Claims C11, C113, C125 represent the main mechanistic conclusion integrating the experimental findings. This is supported by the convergence of evidence showing: (1) IFN-I inhibits LC ADAM17 activity, (2) anti-IFNAR restores activity, (3) anti-IFNAR reduces photosensitivity in an EGFR- and LC ADAM17-dependent manner, and (4) IFN-I reduces ROS, a known ADAM17 activator. The inference is well-supported by the data, though the authors appropriately use cautious language ('at least in part', 'suggest').

result: Anifrolumab may ameliorate lupus skin disease in part by restoring LC ADAM17 sheddase function, and IFNAR blockade should prevent new lesion formation and treat existing lesions if physiologic IFN levels are preserved.
evaluation: Claims C12 and C122 are speculative extrapolations from the mouse data to human therapeutic implications. While the mouse experiments with anti-IFNAR support the mechanism, direct evidence that anifrolumab works through this mechanism in human patients is not provided. The authors appropriately frame these as possibilities ('raise the possibility', 'should'), but clinical validation would be needed to support these claims.

result: The shared pathogenic mechanisms across murine models and human lupus, particularly LC ADAM17 sheddase dysfunction, establish these models as useful for studying lupus skin pathophysiology and identify LC ADAM17 function as a therapeutic target.
evaluation: Claims C112, C126, C129 are supported by the consistent findings across human DLE and three murine models showing IFN signatures and LC ADAM17 dysfunction. The uncoupling of sheddase activity from protein expression and cell numbers (Table 1) across all models and interventions strongly supports LC ADAM17 function as a key contributor. The inference about model utility is reasonable given the shared mechanisms demonstrated.

result: A proposed pathogenic model suggests keratinocyte-derived IFN-I causes LC ADAM17 dysfunction, creating a feed-forward loop leading to keratinocyte damage and lesion formation, with distinct IFN functions in non-lesional (priming) versus lesional (damage) skin.
evaluation: Claims C114-C121 represent a speculative disease model integrating the findings with spatial biology considerations. While the model is consistent with the data (keratinocytes express IFN, LCs are nearby, IFN inhibits LC ADAM17), direct evidence for the feed-forward loop and the proposed distinct functions in non-lesional versus lesional skin is limited. The model is plausible but requires additional experimental validation, particularly regarding keratinocyte-LC interactions and the progression from non-lesional to lesional skin.

result: LC loss is a feature of human lupus skin that is variable in non-lesional skin and more consistent in lesional skin, while LC numbers appear less affected in lupus mouse models.
evaluation: Claims C130-C133 are supported by GSVA analysis of LC gene sets in this manuscript and multiple cited studies. The variability in non-lesional skin and consistency in lesional skin are documented across multiple studies. The comparison between human and mouse models is appropriately cautious, noting that mouse models show less dramatic LC loss. This provides important context for interpreting the model systems.

result: Background on lupus photosensitivity and prior findings that LCs limit photosensitivity via ADAM17-mediated EGFR ligand release, with reduced LC ADAM17 activity in lupus models and patients.
evaluation: Claims C1-C3, C13-C18 represent background information and prior work, primarily from Shipman et al., 2018. These are well-established facts (C1, C13, C14) or findings from the authors' previous work (C2, C3, C15-C18) that provide context for the current study. The claims are appropriately cited and provide the rationale for investigating IFN-I effects on LC ADAM17.

result: Background on IFN signatures in lupus tissues and blood, the importance of IFN-I in disease pathogenesis highlighted by anifrolumab approval, and the IFN-rich environment in non-lesional skin.
evaluation: Claims C19-C26 represent well-established background information supported by multiple citations to published studies and regulatory approval of anifrolumab. These provide the scientific context and rationale for investigating IFN-I effects on LC function in lupus skin. The claims are appropriately cited and establish the importance of IFN-I in lupus pathogenesis.

result: Characterization of the three murine lupus models (MRL/lpr, B6.Sle1yaa, IMQ) including their genetic basis, disease features, and previous findings of LC ADAM17 dysfunction.
evaluation: Claims C45-C56 provide background on the three murine models used in the study. The characterizations are supported by citations to published studies (C45, C50, C56) and the authors' previous work (C46, C47, C51, C54). The new RNAseq data (C52, C53, C55) are appropriately presented with figures. This establishes the models as relevant for studying lupus skin pathophysiology.

result: Background on IFN-I functions in normal skin physiology, ADAM17 biology in other contexts, and IFN-I states in other diseases, providing broader context for the findings.
evaluation: Claims C99, C100, C117, C123, C124, C127, C134-C137 provide broader biological context from published literature. These are appropriately cited and help interpret the findings in the context of normal physiology (IFN-I in wound healing, ADAM17 regulation) and other diseases (interferonopathies, dermatomyositis, checkpoint inhibitor toxicity). This contextualizes the specific findings in lupus.

result: Speculation that modulating ADAM17 enzymatic function offers advantages over controlling transcription/translation or LC numbers for regulating UVR responses.
evaluation: Claim C128 is explicitly speculative ('We speculate') about the biological advantages of regulating enzyme activity versus expression or cell numbers. While the speculation is reasonable given the data showing uncoupling of activity from expression/numbers, it lacks direct experimental support. The authors appropriately frame this as speculation.
